changes.before: Write shelf_label(item, count). Return a string like "Pencil: 1 item" or "Pencil: 3 items". Count is a nonnegative integer. Use "item" only when count equals 1; return the item name unchanged.
changes.after: Build a shelf label from an item name and a count.

before: A shelf label combines a name, a number and a unit. A string is text, while an integer is a whole number. Your function will format these values into one string. Formatting means choosing how values appear as text; it does not change the values stored in the input variables.

An f-string starts with f immediately before its opening quote. Braces { } mark expressions Python should evaluate and insert. A plain quoted string leaves braces as ordinary characters. Use a parameter name inside braces to make the result follow the input on every call.

This complete example inserts two values.
```python
name = "Tape"
rolls = 4
label = f"{name}: {rolls} rolls"
print(label)
```
It prints Tape: 4 rolls. Python converts the number to text within the f-string. The colon and spaces are literal characters that you chose for the label.

Choose the singular word when count == 1. The double equals sign compares values; a single equals sign assigns a value. Zero uses the plural form in this English label. The requirement accepts only nonnegative integer counts, so this exercise does not need to handle negative stock or fractions.

You can choose a word before formatting the final text.
```python
def ticket_label(count):
    word = "ticket" if count == 1 else "tickets"
    return f"{count} {word}"
print(ticket_label(1))
print(ticket_label(0))
```
The output is 1 ticket and 0 tickets. The conditional expression chooses one value. An ordinary if/else block would also work.

return gives the completed label to the caller. print displays something and returns None. Keep shelf_label useful for both screen display and later storage by returning the string. The caller can then decide whether to print it. Preserve punctuation and spaces as stated so labels have a consistent shape.

Test a count of zero, one and several items. Try a two-word name and a name with a non-English letter: the function should carry the name through unchanged. These examples check the boundary where the wording changes. A single sample with three items would not reveal a mistaken singular rule.
after: A shelf label combines a name, a number, and a unit. Your function formats these values into one string. Formatting means choosing how values appear as text; it does not change the input values.

An f-string starts with `f` just before its opening quote. Braces, `{}`, mark values or calculations to put into the text. Put a parameter name inside the braces to use the current input.

Without `f`, braces are ordinary text.

This complete example inserts two values.
```python
name = "Tape"
rolls = 4
label = f"{name}: {rolls} rolls"
print(label)
```
It prints Tape: 4 rolls. Python converts the number to text in the f-string. The colon and spaces appear exactly as written.

Choose the word for one item when `count == 1`. Choose the word for more than one item for zero and every other allowed count.

This exercise accepts whole-number counts of zero or greater. It does not accept negative counts or fractions.

You can choose a word before formatting the final text.
```python
def ticket_label(count):
    word = "ticket" if count == 1 else "tickets"
    return f"{count} {word}"
print(ticket_label(1))
print(ticket_label(0))
```
The output is 1 ticket and 0 tickets. The conditional expression chooses one value. An ordinary if/else block would also work.

`return` gives the finished label back to the code that called the function. That code can choose to display it or save it.

`print` displays a value and gives back `None`. Return the string from `shelf_label` so other code can use it.

Keep the requested punctuation and spaces in the label.

Test counts of zero, one, and several items. Try a two-word name and a name with a non-English letter. The function should carry the name through unchanged. These tests check where the wording changes; one sample with three items would not reveal a mistaken singular rule.

before.question: The label-building function returns text but the caller never prints the returned value. What should you expect in a normal script?
choices: The returned label need not appear on screen
The function must raise an error
before.explanation: Returning makes a value available to the caller. Printing is a separate effect; a script does not automatically display every return value.
